title: Basic Sentence Structure (SVO & Verb-Zweit-Regel)
subtitle: The fundamental Verb-at-Position-2 rule and standard word order
summary: Master the most essential rule of German syntax: in declarative sentences (statements), the conjugated verb is strictly locked at Position 2 (V2 Rule), while subjects and time adverbs can move.

explanation_payload.text: In German declarative statements, word order revolves around one absolute law: The conjugated verb MUST be at Position 2 (Verb-Zweit-Stellung). While standard statements start with Subject + Verb + Object (SVO) just like English, German is flexible with Position 1—if you put time, place, or an object first, the verb stays at Position 2 and the Subject moves right behind it (Inversion).
bullet_points: Position 1 (Vorfeld): The element in focus — usually the Subject (Ich), a Time expression (Heute), or Place (In Berlin).
Position 2 (Verb-Position): The conjugated action verb — STRICTLY LOCKED here in all normal statements!
Position 3 / Mittelfeld: The Subject (if not at Pos 1), followed by Objects and additional information.

table_payload.footnote: Egal was auf Position 1 steht: Das konjugierte Verb bleibt IMMER unverrückbar auf Position 2!

exception_payload.description: The coordinating conjunctions Aber, Denn, Und, Sondern, Oder (ADUSO) connect main clauses and take Position 0. They DO NOT count as Position 1 and do not trigger inversion.
example_sentences: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn [0] ich [1] wohne [2] in Frankfurt.
Er ist müde, aber [0] er [1] arbeitet [2] fleißig weiter.
Wir bleiben zu Hause und [0] wir [1] kochen [2] gemeinsam.

example_payload.german: Ich lerne jeden Tag neue Wörter.
example_payload.english: I learn new words every day.

example_payload.german: Heute lerne ich Deutsch mit Takt.
example_payload.english: Today I am learning German with Takt.

example_payload.german: Am Wochenende fahren wir nach München.
example_payload.english: On the weekend we are driving to Munich.
example_payload.note: Prepositional phrase 'Am Wochenende' fills Position 1; verb 'fahren' stays in Position 2.

example_payload.german: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, sondern ich trinke Tee.
example_payload.english: I don't drink coffee, but rather I drink tea.
example_payload.note: 'sondern' occupies Position 0, followed by standard SVO.

tip_payload.title: Die 2-Finger-Zählmethode
tip_payload.content: Whenever you start a sentence with anything other than the subject (like 'Gestern...', 'Manchmal...', 'Hier...'), immediately place the verb next! Count on your fingers: [1: Gestern] [2: habe] [3: ich]... Never say 'Gestern ich habe...'!

title: Personal Pronouns & Regular Verb Endings
subtitle: Mastering ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie and the present tense formula
summary: Learn all 9 German personal pronouns in the Nominative case and master the regular verb conjugation pattern (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en) with stem changes and phonetic rules.

explanation_payload.text: Personal pronouns replace nouns (e.g. 'der Tisch' → 'er', 'die Frau' → 'sie'). In German, verbs change their ending depending on WHO is performing the action. To conjugate a regular verb, remove '-en' from the infinitive to find the stem (Verbstamm), then attach the personal ending matching the pronoun.
bullet_points: Informal vs. Formal: Use 'du' for 1 friend/child, 'ihr' for 2+ friends/children, and capital 'Sie' for adults, strangers, and professional settings.
3rd Person Genders: 'er' replaces masculine nouns (der Mann → er), 'sie' replaces feminine nouns (die Frau → sie), 'es' replaces neuter nouns (das Kind → es).
Verb Endings Pattern: The classic rhyme: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en!

table_payload.footnote: Merk-Reim für die Endungen: E - ST - T - EN - T - EN (E-St-T-En-T-En)!

exception_payload.description: When the verb stem ends in -t or -d, add an extra '-e-' before '-st' and '-t' to make it pronounceable.
When the stem ends in a sibilant (-s, -ß, -z), the 'du' form takes only '-t' instead of '-st'.
The two essential irregular verbs must be memorized completely.
example_sentences: sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind
haben: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben

example_payload.german: Ich lerne seit drei Monaten Deutsch.
example_payload.english: I have been learning German for three months.

example_payload.german: Woher kommst du und wo wohnst du?
example_payload.english: Where are you from and where do you live?

example_payload.german: Er arbeitet heute im Homeoffice.
example_payload.english: He is working from home today.

example_payload.german: Wir haben heute Abend viel Zeit.
example_payload.english: We have plenty of time this evening.

example_payload.german: Wie heißen Sie, Herr Müller?
example_payload.english: What is your name, Mr. Müller?
example_payload.note: Formal 'Sie' is always capitalized and takes '-en'.

tip_payload.title: Das 'sie/Sie'-Trio sofort unterscheiden
tip_payload.content: Look at the verb ending and capitalization: 'sie lernt' (ending -t) = she; 'sie lernen' (lowercase + ending -en) = they; 'Sie lernen' (capitalized + ending -en) = formal You. The verb ending always clarifies the subject!

title: Question Formation: Ja/Nein & W-Fragen
subtitle: How to build Yes/No questions, W-Questions, and using 'Doch!'
summary: Master asking questions in German: Ja/Nein-Fragen (verb jumps to Position 1), W-Fragen (Question word + Verb at Position 2), and how to answer negative questions with the magic word 'Doch!'.

explanation_payload.text: German questions are structured in two clear ways depending on the type of answer expected:
bullet_points: 1. Ja/Nein-Fragen (Yes/No Questions): The conjugated verb jumps to Position 1 (Verb-Erst-Stellung / VSO). Answer with Ja, Nein, or Doch.
2. W-Fragen (Information Questions): Start with a W-Word (Was, Woher, Wie, Wo) at Position 1, followed immediately by the Verb at Position 2, then the Subject.
3. The Magic Word 'Doch!': If asked a negative question ('Trinkst du keinen Kaffee?'), use 'Doch!' to contradict the negative and say 'Yes I do!'.

table_payload.footnote: Merkhilfe: Wo (Standort), Woher (Herkunft mit 'aus'), Wohin (Zielrichtung mit 'nach/in')!

exception_payload.description: If a question contains a negation ('nicht' or 'kein'), you CANNOT answer with 'Ja' to mean 'Yes I do'. Use 'Doch!' to overturn the negation.
example_sentences: Frage: Trinkst du keinen Kaffee? → Antwort: Doch! (Ich trinke gerne Kaffee.)
Frage: Hast du heute keine Zeit? → Antwort: Doch, ich habe Zeit!
Frage: Kommst du heute nicht? → Antwort: Nein, ich komme nicht. (Bestätigt Verneinung)

example_payload.german: Sprichst du Deutsch? – Ja, ich lerne es gerade.
example_payload.english: Do you speak German? – Yes, I am currently learning it.

example_payload.german: Woher kommen Sie? – Ich komme aus der Schweiz.
example_payload.english: Where are you from? – I come from Switzerland.

example_payload.german: Hast du heute keinen Hunger? – Doch, ich habe großen Hunger!
example_payload.english: Aren't you hungry today? – Yes, I am very hungry!

example_payload.german: Wohin fahrt ihr im Sommer? – Wir fahren an die Ostsee.
example_payload.english: Where are you going in summer? – We are going to the Baltic Sea.

tip_payload.title: Wo vs. Woher vs. Wohin merken
tip_payload.content: Pair the question word with the typical preposition in the answer: 'Wo? → in / bei' (Wo bist du? – Im Büro), 'Woher? → aus / von' (Woher kommst du? – Aus Spanien), 'Wohin? → nach / zu' (Wohin gehst du? – Nach Hause).

title: Noun Genders & Articles (Der, Die, Das)
subtitle: Definite, Indefinite, and Negative Articles in the Nominative + Noun Suffix Secrets
summary: Master the three German grammatical genders (der, die, das), learn indefinite articles (ein/eine), negative articles (kein/keine), and discover reliable suffix patterns that tell you the gender automatically.

explanation_payload.text: Unlike English which only uses 'the' and 'a', every German noun has a grammatical gender: Masculine (der), Feminine (die), or Neuter (das). In addition, German nouns are ALWAYS capitalized without exception (der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch).
bullet_points: Bestimmter Artikel (Definite): der (m), die (f), das (n), Plural: die (for all genders).
Unbestimmter Artikel (Indefinite): ein (m), eine (f), ein (n). No plural form exists for 'ein'!
Negativartikel (Negative): kein (m), keine (f), kein (n), Plural: keine (all genders).
Golden Rule: Always learn the noun together with its article and plural form: 'der Tisch, -e'!

table_payload.footnote: Achtung: Unbestimmte Artikel ('ein/eine') haben KEINE Pluralform! Für Negation im Plural nutzt man 'keine'.

sections.title: Suffix-Geheimnisse: Wie man das Geschlecht erkennt

rows: die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Möglichkeit, die Nation
das Mädchen, das Dokument, das Museum, das Essen
der Optimismus, der Schmetterling, der Motor, der Montag
table_payload.footnote: Lerne besonders die femininen Endungen (-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion) — sie sind fast ausnahmslos feminin!

exception_payload.description: Because '-chen' is a diminutive neuter suffix, all words with '-chen' are grammatically NEUTER (das Mädchen, das Brötchen, das Hähnchen), regardless of biology.

exception_payload.rule_name: Zusammengesetzte Nomen (Komposita): Das letzte Wort entscheidet!
exception_payload.description: In compound nouns, the LAST noun ALWAYS determines the gender and the plural form of the whole compound word.
example_sentences: die Hand + der Schuh = DER Handschuh (the glove)
das Auto + die Tür = DIE Autotür (the car door)
der Tisch + das Tuch = DAS Tischtuch (the tablecloth)

example_payload.german: Das ist ein Tisch. Der Tisch ist modern.
example_payload.english: That is a table. The table is modern.
example_payload.note: First mentioned with indefinite 'ein', then referenced with definite 'der'.

example_payload.german: Ich habe eine Frage, aber ich habe keine Antwort.
example_payload.english: I have a question, but I have no answer.

example_payload.german: Das Mädchen liest die Zeitung im Wohnzimmer.
example_payload.english: The girl is reading the newspaper in the living room.

example_payload.german: Der Apfelbaum steht in unserem Garten.
example_payload.english: The apple tree stands in our garden.
example_payload.note: Compound noun: der Apfel + der Baum → DER Apfelbaum.

tip_payload.title: Die 3-Farben-Methode für Vokabeln
tip_payload.content: Never learn a noun without its article! Color-code your vocabulary: BLUE for 'der' (der Tisch), RED for 'die' (die Lampe), and GREEN for 'das' (das Buch). In German, the article is an inseparable part of the word.

title: Numbers, Counting & Age (Zahlen & Alter)
subtitle: Mastering 0–100, the reversed tens/ones rule, and telling age & prices
summary: Master German numbers from 0 to 100, understand the teen pattern (-zehn) and the famous inverted compound pattern (eins-und-zwanzig = one-and-twenty), and learn to state age, prices, and telephone numbers.

explanation_payload.text: The German number system has three core building blocks:
bullet_points: 1. Grundzahlen (0–12): Unique root words that must be memorized (null, eins, zwei, drei ... elf, zwölf).
2. Teen Numbers (13–19): Combine digit + 'zehn' (dreizehn, vierzehn...). Notice: 16 (sechzehn) and 17 (siebzehn) drop letters!
3. Tens Numbers (20–90): End in '-zig' (zwanzig, vierzig...), except for 30 which is 'dreißig' (with 'ß').
4. The Reverse Rule (21–99): In German, you say the ONES digit first, then 'und', then the TENS digit (24 = vier-und-zwanzig = four-and-twenty)!

table_payload.footnote: Achtung bei 16 (sechzehn) und 17 (siebzehn): Das -s bzw. -en fällt weg!
Zahlen unter 1 Million werden im Deutschen als EIN einziges Wort zusammengeschrieben: fünfunddreißig!

exception_payload.description: Alone the number is 'eins', but inside compound numbers it drops the '-s' to become 'ein'.
30 is the ONLY tens number spelled with '-ßig' (dreißig). All others use '-zig' (zwanzig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig...).
6 (sechs) drops '-s' in 16 (sechzehn) and 60 (sechzig). 7 (sieben) drops '-en' in 17 (siebzehn) and 70 (siebzig).

example_payload.german: Wie alt bist du? – Ich bin 24 (vierundzwanzig) Jahre alt.
example_payload.english: How old are you? – I am 24 years old.

example_payload.german: Meine Handynummer ist 0176 543219.
example_payload.english: My mobile number is 0176 543219.
example_payload.note: Phone numbers in German are spoken digit by digit: null, eins, sieben, sechs...

example_payload.german: Das Buch kostet 14,90 Euro (vierzehn Euro neunzig).
example_payload.english: The book costs 14.90 Euros (fourteen euros ninety).
example_payload.note: Prices place the currency word between euros and cents.

example_payload.german: In unserem Deutschkurs sind 18 (achtzehn) Teilnehmer.
example_payload.english: In our German class there are 18 participants.

tip_payload.title: Die Uhrzeiger-Regel: Von rechts nach links lesen!
tip_payload.content: In English you say 'twenty-four' (tens then ones). In German you say 'vierundzwanzig' (four-and-twenty). When reading a 2-digit number, look at the last digit first, say it, add 'und', and then say the tens digit: 24 = 4 and 20 (vier-und-zwanzig)!

title: Das Perfekt mit 'haben' und 'sein'
subtitle: Speaking about completed actions in the past
summary: The Perfekt is the primary past tense used in spoken German. It uses a helping verb (haben or sein) at Position 2 and a Partizip II at the end of the sentence.

explanation_payload.text: The choice between 'haben' and 'sein' depends on the nature of the main verb:
bullet_points: SEIN: Used for verbs of MOVEMENT from A to B (fahren, gehen, fliegen, kommen) or CHANGE OF STATE (einschlafen, aufstehen, passieren). Also used with 'sein' and 'bleiben'.
HABEN: Used for all transitive verbs (verbs taking an object), reflexive verbs, and static actions (arbeiten, lernen, essen, kaufen).

table_payload.footnote: Remember: Verben ending in '-ieren' NEVER get a 'ge-' prefix!

exception_payload.description: Verbs starting with be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss- DO NOT take 'ge-' in Partizip II.

example_payload.german: Ich habe heute morgen einen Kaffee getrunken.
example_payload.english: I drank a coffee this morning.
example_payload.note: Static action with direct object → uses 'haben'.

example_payload.german: Gestern sind wir nach Berlin gefahren.
example_payload.english: Yesterday we drove to Berlin.
example_payload.note: Movement from A to B → uses 'sein' ('sind').

example_payload.german: Um wie viel Uhr bist du aufgestanden?
example_payload.english: At what time did you get up?

tip_payload.title: Bewegung von A nach B
tip_payload.content: For 'sein', it's not just any movement—it must be a movement from Point A to Point B! 'Ich bin nach Spanien geflogen' (A to B) uses SEIN, but 'Ich habe im Pool geschwommen' (staying in the pool) uses HABEN.

title: Modalverben im Präteritum
subtitle: Talking about past obligations, permissions, and wishes
summary: In spoken and written German, we use the Präteritum (Simple Past) for Modal Verbs instead of the Perfekt. Learn how umlauts disappear and verbs conjugate in the past.

sections.title: Wann benutzt man das? (When to use it)

explanation_payload.text: When speaking about the past in German, most verbs use 'Perfekt' (e.g. 'Ich habe gemacht'). However, Modal Verbs are an exception! We almost ALWAYS use Präteritum for Modal Verbs in spoken and written German.
bullet_points: müssen → obligation in the past (had to)
können → ability / opportunity in the past (could / was able to)
dürfen → permission in the past (was allowed to)
wollen → desire / intention in the past (wanted to)
sollen → recommendation / assignment in the past (was supposed to)
mögen → liking in the past (liked / cared for)

formula_payload.formula_structure: Subject + Conjugated Modal Verb (Pos 2) + ... + Infinitive Verb (Satzende)

table_payload.footnote: Notice: 'ich' and 'er/sie/es' forms are ALWAYS identical in Modal Verb Präteritum!

exception_payload.description: Verbs with umlauts in present tense (müssen, können, dürfen, mögen) LOSE their umlauts in Präteritum.
example_sentences: Präsens: Ich muss heute früh aufstehen. → Präteritum: Ich musste gestern früh aufstehen.
Präsens: Wir können nicht kommen. → Präteritum: Wir konnten nicht kommen.
Präsens: Er darf kein Eis essen. → Präteritum: Er durfte kein Eis essen.

example_payload.german: In der Schule musste ich eine Schuluniform tragen.
example_payload.english: In school, I had to wear a school uniform.
example_payload.note: Modal verb 'musste' at Position 2, Infinitive 'tragen' at the end.

example_payload.german: Früher konnte ich jeden Nachmittag meine Freunde treffen.
example_payload.english: In the past, I was able to meet my friends every afternoon.

example_payload.german: Am Abend durften wir nicht lange draußen bleiben.
example_payload.english: In the evening, we were not allowed to stay outside for long.

tip_payload.title: Stolperfalle: 'möchten' vs 'wollten'
tip_payload.content: There is no Präteritum form for 'möchten'. 'Möchten' is technically a subjunctive form of 'mögen'. If you want to say 'I wanted to...' in the past, ALWAYS use 'wollte' (from 'wollen'). Never say 'ich mochte...' when you mean 'wanted'!

title: Nebensätze mit 'weil'
subtitle: Expressing reasons and cause-and-effect in German
summary: The conjunction 'weil' (because) creates a subordinate clause (Nebensatz) and sends the conjugated verb to the absolute end of the sentence.

sections.title: Wann benutzt man das? (When to use it)

explanation_payload.text: We use 'weil' to answer questions starting with 'Warum?' (Why?). 'Weil' connects a main clause (Hauptsatz) with a reason clause (Nebensatz).
bullet_points: Hauptsatz: Contains the main statement.
Weil-Nebensatz: Explains WHY the main statement happens.
Rule: A comma MUST separate the Hauptsatz and the Nebensatz!

formula_payload.formula_structure: Hauptsatz [Verb Pos 2] , + weil + Subjekt + ... + Konjugiertes Verb (SATZENDE)

example_payload.german: Lea kann nicht kommen, weil sie ihren Vater besucht.
example_payload.english: Lea cannot come because she is visiting her father.
example_payload.note: Verb 'besucht' conjugated for 'sie' moves to the end.

example_payload.german: Marvin kommt später, weil er heute arbeiten muss.
example_payload.english: Marvin is coming later because he has to work today.
example_payload.note: With a modal verb, the conjugated modal ('muss') goes to the VERY END after the infinitive ('arbeiten').

tip_payload.title: Kurzantwort auf 'Warum?'
tip_payload.content: If someone asks 'Warum isst du nichts?' (Why aren't you eating?), you don't need to repeat the main clause. You can answer directly starting with 'weil': 'Weil ich keinen Hunger habe.'

title: Wechselpräpositionen (Two-Way Prepositions)
subtitle: Akkusativ vs. Dativ: Wohin? (Movement) vs. Wo? (Location)
summary: Nine prepositions can take either Akkusativ or Dativ depending on whether you express movement toward a destination (Wohin?) or static location (Wo?).

explanation_payload.text: The 9 dual-case prepositions are: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen.
bullet_points: WOHIN? (Direction / Movement to target) → AKKUSATIV (den / die / das / die)
WO? (Location / Static position) → DATIV (dem / der / dem / den + n)

blocks.label: Subjekt + Verb + Akkusativ
blocks.example_word: Ich stelle das Buch auf den Tisch.

blocks.label: Subjekt + Verb + Dativ
blocks.example_word: Das Buch steht auf dem Tisch.

table_payload.footnote: Action verbs (stellen, legen, setzen) are ALWAYS regular! State verbs (stehen, liegen, sitzen) are irregular.

example_payload.german: Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch.
example_payload.english: I put the mobile phone onto the table.
example_payload.note: Akkusativ ('den Tisch') because it's a movement towards a surface (Wohin?).

example_payload.german: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
example_payload.english: The mobile phone is lying on the table.
example_payload.note: Dativ ('dem Tisch') because it describes a static location (Wo?).

tip_payload.title: Kompakte Verschmelzungen (Contractions)
tip_payload.content: In spoken German, we almost always contract: in + das = ins, an + das = ans, in + dem = im, an + dem = am, zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur.
